class.name: PhysXHair3D
class.brief_description: Strand hair that moves: a [HairGroom]'s strands simulated on the GPU and drawn as fibres.
class.description: Simulates every strand of [member groom] with compute shaders, so it runs on any GPU the renderer supports (no CUDA needed). The node is the head: the groom is in its space and the roots follow it, so put it under a [BoneAttachment3D] on the head bone. Strands fall under gravity against the air, blow in the [member wind] and its eddies, keep their groomed shape and length, and stay out of the [member collision_spheres]. The solver is a port of AMD TressFX 4.1's (MIT), with its parameters and defaults in metres and seconds. A share of the strands ([member guide_ratio]) is simulated as guides and the rest follow them. Each guide is a chain of points whose first two are pinned to the head. Every substep the other points take a damped step under gravity and the air ([member damping]), the part near the root is pulled toward the groomed pose ([member global_stiffness] over [member global_range]), the head's motion carries the strand along (velocity shock propagation, [member vsp_coeff]), each segment is turned back toward its groomed angle to its parent ([member local_stiffness]), the segments are put back to their rest lengths, points inside the spheres are pushed out and stopped, and the speed is clamped ([member max_speed]). Strands don't collide with each other. The strands are rebuilt in the vertex shader straight from the simulated positions on the GPU (no CPU readback). In raster they are drawn as AMD TressFX does: one ribbon per strand facing the camera, widened to at least about 0.7 px a side, with its opacity cut to the share of the pixel the real strand covers (coverage), alpha blended. The strands are sorted far to near from the camera every frame on the GPU, so the blend is in order and the hair is smooth without TAA or MSAA. The shadow maps keep the same share of their texels, so the hair shadows itself. Under path tracing they are the real-width crossed strips of [HairMesh] and shade as hair fibres (the Chiang 2016 model, with [member melanin] for the colour). To draw them your own way, set [member render_material]: a [ShaderMaterial] whose shader reads the [code]hair_positions[/code] texture like the built-in one (strands in draw order, a fixed number of texels each; [code]w[/code] is the share along the strand, or [code]-1[/code] past its end) and sets [code]HAIR[/code], [code]HAIR_ABSORPTION[/code] and [code]HAIR_ROUGHNESS[/code]; the [code]IN_PATH_TRACER[/code] built-in tells its path tracer pass from raster. In the editor the groom is drawn still. The simulation runs only in a running game.

method.name: get_screen_size
method.description: The hair's screen size from the current camera: its bounding sphere's diameter over the view's height. See [member card_screen_size].

method.name: is_drawing_cards
method.description: Returns [code]true[/code] while the hair is drawn as cards (see [member cards_enabled]).

method.name: reset_simulation
method.description: Puts every strand back in its groomed pose on the head, at rest. Call it after teleporting the character.

members.member: How many cards the strands are clustered into. Each card is two crossed strips.
How far from the camera, in metres, the strands give way to cards, when [member card_screen_size] is [code]0[/code].

The screen size below which the strands give way to cards: the hair's bounding sphere's diameter over the view's height (as Unreal Engine's groom LODs), whatever the distance, field of view or resolution. Cards stand in for clumps of strands and show as strips when large on screen, so a zoomed-in camera keeps the strands. [code]0.07[/code] matches about 15 m with a 75 degree field of view for a head of long hair. [code]0[/code]: switch by [member card_distance] instead. [method get_screen_size] gives the hair's current screen size.

How long, in seconds, the strands and cards cross-fade when the hair switches between them: the cards fade in over the strands, then the strands fade out beneath them, so the switch shows no step. [code]0[/code]: switch in one frame. The path tracer always switches at once.

If [code]true[/code], hair cards are baked from the groom when the hair is built (shared by every node with the same groom and settings), and past [member card_distance] the hair is drawn as cards instead of strands: textured strips along clumps of strands, which move with the same guide strands. Only the guides and the cards are then simulated, so distant hair costs a small fraction of strands. Raster only: while the environment path traces, the hair stays strands at every distance.

The strands cast into the shadow maps, so the hair shades the face, neck and shoulders under it and the ground. Godot leaves blended materials out of the shadow maps, so a copy of the strands is drawn there alone, each strand at its own share of texels (stochastic transparency). Not with [member render_material] set, nor while cards are drawn; the path tracer traces the strands themselves.
How far, in metres, the strands rest above [member collision_cloth]'s simulated surface (on top of the collision margin): the cloth's own thickness.

A [MeshInstance3D] the strands stay out of, as AMD TressFX's SDF collision: every frame its triangles (skinned on the CPU when it has a [Skin], else placed by its transform) build a signed distance field around them on the GPU (seeded by the triangles, filled by jump flooding), and points inside the body or closer than the margin are pushed out along it and stop. Use a closed, low-poly proxy of the body (shoulders, neck, back; a few thousand triangles). Empty: only [member collision_spheres].
The cell of [member collision_body]'s distance field, in metres. Grown when the body is too large for 64 cells a side.

A [PhysXSkinnedCloth3D] the strands rest on (a collar, a hood, a coat's shoulders): its simulated triangles join [member collision_body]'s distance field each frame, read on the GPU from the cloth's own positions, so hair lies on the cloth as it moves and does not pass through it. The cloth's outside is the side its mesh normals face: strands that start under it near its surface are put back on top, as hair lies over clothes, and kept [member cloth_thickness] off it. Empty: none.

Spheres the strands stay out of, in this node's space: [code]x, y, z[/code] the centre and [code]w[/code] the radius. Usually the skull, the neck and the shoulders. Up to 32. For a body shape spheres fit badly, see [member collision_body].

How fast a point's velocity relaxes toward the air's: each substep it keeps [code]exp(-damping * 60 * dt)[/code] of the difference (TressFX's damping). In still air this slows the hair; in [member wind] it is how quickly the hair takes up the wind. Hair is light enough that air, not its weight, sets how it moves: higher is floatier, lower is heavier and swings longer.
The [DirectionalLight3D] [member deep_shadows] are built toward. Empty: the brightest shadowed [DirectionalLight3D] in the scene, found by itself.

With [member deep_shadows], how many shadowed [OmniLight3D] and [SpotLight3D] nodes get a deep opacity map of their own: the ones that light the hair most (energy times falloff at the hair's centre), found in the scene by themselves. Each map is a perspective view from the light that just holds the hair, and costs about as much as the directional light's. A light inside the hair's bounding sphere gets none. [code]0[/code]: only the directional light, as before.

With [member hair_shading], the strands shade themselves from the directional light ([member deep_shadow_light]) and the main omni and spot lights ([member deep_shadow_local_lights]) with deep opacity maps (Yuksel and Keyser 2008, as Unreal Engine's hair): each frame the solver records, from the light, where the first hair is, how much hair lies in three layers past it, and where the collision spheres and [member collision_body] are, and each strand takes the light that passes the hair and head in front of it. The self-shadow is smooth instead of the shadow map's grain, and light thins through the hair as through real hair. The hair still casts into the shadow map for everything else, each strand at its own share of texels (stochastic transparency), so a shadow behind several strands builds up as their product. Other lights shadow the hair through the shadow maps as before (and lose the hair's self-shadow from them when a map's light shares their kind, as their shadow lookups move past the hair too). Off: the shadow maps alone, as before. [b]Note:[/b] the head counts only through [member collision_spheres] and [member collision_body]; something opaque inside the hair that neither covers does not shadow the hair from that light.
Seconds the hair takes to dry from soaked when no rain falls on it, at an even rate.
The gravity used when [member use_world_gravity] is off.
How much of each strand, from the root, [member global_stiffness] acts on, so the hair stays styled at the scalp and swings free below. Raise it for short or styled hair.
How strongly the points within [member global_range] are pulled toward their groomed pose on the head, per 1/60 s (TressFX's global shape constraint).

The share of strands that are grey: grown with no melanin, only the keratin's own faint yellow left (canities). Each strand is grey or not by its own seed, so grey hairs show singly among the coloured ones. Cards mix the share into each clump's colour.
The strands, in this node's space.

The share of strands that are simulated (guide hairs, as in HairWorks and TressFX). Every other strand follows its three nearest guides, keeping its own groomed curl, so the hair moves in clumps like real hair and the simulation costs a tenth. [code]1[/code] simulates every strand on its own.
How much the wind varies over time and from strand to strand, so the hair flutters instead of leaning stiffly.

Lights the strands in raster with the Marschner hair model as Unreal Engine evaluates it (Karis 2016): the white highlight, the coloured second highlight, light through the fibres when lit from behind, and multiple scattering, so the side away from the light is lit through the hair instead of falling black. Strands also let part of the light through in shadow maps (dual scattering's forward transmittance, Zinke et al. 2008): blonde hair more, dark hair less. Off, the strands take Godot's standard anisotropic lighting and block light fully. The path tracer always uses its own hair fibre shading.
How many times per substep the segments are put back to their rest lengths. More keeps long hair from stretching.
How many times per substep [member local_stiffness] is applied.

How strongly each segment keeps its groomed angle to its parent, so bends, waves and curls stay in (TressFX's local shape constraint; halved and capped at 0.95 inside, as TressFX does). [code]0[/code] hangs like rope.

Distance level of detail, as AMD TressFX: between [member lod_start_distance] and [member lod_end_distance] from the camera, the rasterizer draws a shrinking random share of the strands, down to [member lod_strand_ratio], and widens the rest so the hair keeps its opacity. Far away, strands are thinner than a pixel, so fewer, wider ones look the same for less fill. The simulation and the path tracer always keep every strand at its real width. Off, every strand is drawn at any distance.
The camera distance (metres, to this node) at and beyond which only [member lod_strand_ratio] of the strands are drawn.
The camera distance (metres, to this node) within which every strand is drawn.
The share of the strands drawn at [member lod_end_distance] and beyond, each widened by its inverse.
The fastest a point may move, in m/s, so a sudden jump of the head doesn't fling the hair.
The hair colour as melanin concentration: [code]0[/code] white, [code]0.1[/code] to [code]0.25[/code] blonde to light brown, [code]0.5[/code] brown, [code]0.9[/code] and above black.
The share of red melanin (pheomelanin), from brown and black hair at [code]0[/code] to red and auburn hair.
How rough the fibres are around their axis, which spreads the highlight across the strand (path tracing only).
A material of your own to draw the strands with, instead of the built-in one.
The width of a strand at the root, in metres. A real hair is 0.00005 to 0.0001 m; drawn strands are wider so fewer of them cover the head.
How rough the fibres are along their length: low gives a tight, bright highlight.

Where a groomed strand runs straight, the strands are drawn (raster and path traced) through fewer of its points: Douglas-Peucker on the groomed strand, as Unreal Engine's groom decimation, keeping every point the strand would otherwise stray from by more than this share of [member root_width]. Below a strand's own width the drawn hair looks the same, with fewer triangles for the path tracer to refit and fewer vertices to shade. Every point still simulates. Wavy, curly and frizzy grooms keep most of their points. [code]0[/code]: every point is drawn.
When off, the strands hold their last pose relative to the head.

How much snow lies on the hair: [code]0[/code] none, [code]1[/code] as much as [member snow_capacity] holds. It settles on the top layer, where no hair above shields it, and on the side the wind drives it at; each covered strand point carries a small white clump of crystals. Set by snowfall when [member weather_wetting] is on (snow is caught more slowly as the load fills), it melts above freezing and from the head's warmth, and the melt water wets the hair. Can be set directly.
Millimetres of snow (as water) the hair holds when [member snow] is [code]1[/code].

Keeps the guide strands from passing through each other: once a frame their points are hashed into a grid and pushed apart where two strands come closer than [member strand_collision_radius] (position based, as Müller et al. 2007, with averaged corrections as Macklin et al. 2014). The follower strands take their places from the guides, so they follow. Works with the hair volume, which keeps the hair's overall density.
How much of the sliding between two touching guide strands is removed. [code]0[/code]: they slide freely; [code]1[/code]: they stick.
How close two guide strands may come, in metres. Each guide stands for a lock of follower strands, so this is a lock's thickness rather than a single hair's.
Solver steps per frame. More keeps long hair stiffer and fast heads cleaner, at a small GPU cost.

How much sunlight has lightened the hair, from [code]0[/code] (none) to [code]1[/code]. Light breaks the dark melanin (eumelanin) down faster than the red (pheomelanin), so the lengths that have grown out longest, toward the tips, turn lighter and warmer, from about a fifth of the way down.

If [code]true[/code], hair drawn as cards (see [member cards_enabled]) draws each clump as one thick strand instead of two textured strips: a strip facing the camera as wide as the clump's cross-section seen from there, as opaque as its strands' total width, and shaded as the clump (its fibres shadowing and masking one another, as Huang et al.'s thick strands, EGSR 2025). Its colour matches the strands where the textured cards read bluish low by about a fifth. The switch is per segment: a stretch of strands whose clump is at most 2 pixels across draws as that clump's thick strand, so the hair hands over a few clumps at a time as it recedes, with no cross-fade (see [member card_transition]). [code]false[/code]: textured cards, switched in for the whole hair by [member card_screen_size].
The width of a strand at the tip, in metres.

Eddies in the [member wind], as a share of its speed. The eddies are carried along with the wind, so neighbouring strands flutter together and each strand ripples along its length. [code]0[/code] blows the hair as one sheet.
The size of the [member turbulence] eddies, in metres.
Use the world's gravity (from the physics settings) instead of [member fixed_gravity].

Strands push and drag on each other through a grid around the groom, as Petrovic, Henne and Anderson 2005 (Pixar): each frame the guide strands' density and velocity are gathered into 32 cells a side, and every point is pulled toward its neighbours' mean velocity ([member volume_friction]) and pushed out of hair packed denser than the groom ([member volume_stiffness]). The hair keeps its volume when it falls or blows instead of packing flat, and moves as a mass rather than as loose strands. Off: strands pass through each other, as before.
How much each point takes up its neighbours' mean velocity, per 1/60 s. Higher makes the hair move more as one mass.
How hard hair packed denser than the groom pushes apart, in m²/s² per unit of excess density. Higher keeps more volume.
The root acceleration, in m/s², above which the hair is carried with the head entirely ([member vsp_coeff] taken as [code]1[/code]), so a very fast turn doesn't overstretch it.

How much of the head's motion each substep carries the whole strand, and its velocity, along (TressFX's velocity shock propagation). [code]0[/code] leaves the hair to catch up by itself; higher keeps it with the head when the character turns or runs.
Millimetres of rain that soak the hair: at 5 mm/h with the default the hair is soaked in 12 minutes.

If [code]true[/code], precipitation from the active [WeatherMap3D] reaches the hair (less what a canopy catches, none under a roof found by a ray up from the hair) and it dries when that stops. The weather map splits it into rain, which wets the hair at once, and snow, which settles as [member snow] and wets it as it melts. With no weather map, or no rain, the hair stays as [member wetness] is set.
If [code]true[/code] and a [WeatherMap3D] is in the scene, its wind at this node (mean wind plus gusts) is added to [member wind].
How far wet strands gather onto their guide strands, from a little past the root out to the tips. [code]0[/code]: wet hair keeps its groomed spread.

How wet the hair is: [code]0[/code] dry, [code]1[/code] soaked. Wet hair is darker and glossier, heavier (less blown by the wind), softer (hangs flatter) and gathers into clumps. Set by rain when [member weather_wetting] is on, and can be set directly.
The air's velocity in world space, in m/s. Strands take up its velocity at the rate set by [member damping]; a head moving through still air is slowed the same way.
